 Price & Siffre’s latest cases position them as the champions of the underdog, but one of them could make a whole industry bleed.
 Photo: Elizabeth Fisher/CBS 
 In last week’s Cupertino premiere, Michael pitched Olivia the mission statement for their new Silicon Valley law firm, Price & Siffre. They’re going to provide a voice in court for all of the Davids who are getting pushed around by the tech Goliaths. That sounds noble! … In theory, anyway. In Cupertino ’s second episode, we get a better look at what that means in practice — and we get our first real sense of how this show’s going to work, now that the intros and origins are out of the way.
 Early in “Vik & Bo,” Michael makes his pitch again to an old friend, from whom he’s asking for a loan. This time, Michael sounds less idealistic and much more cynical. With a sly, knowing tone, he says that he sees Price & Siffre as a profit-generating pest, “Small enough to shake some cash loose in settlements, and not so big they feel they need to squash us.” If anything, they’ll only make some corporate evildoers mad for a day.
 And yet! Despite the episode’s binary title, Price & Siffre are presented with three new cases this week; in at least one of them, they are very much positioned as the champions of the underdog, while the other … well, it could make a whole industry bleed.
 Let’s start with the Vik part of “Vik & Bo.” We actually met Vik (Nik Dodani) at the end of the premiere, when he came barging into the Price & Siffre offices desperate and disheveled. The reason he’s all mussed up is that he jumped out of a second-story bathroom window in the office building across the street, fleeing a deposition. Vik is a programmer for Moon Chaser, a company that puts on drone light shows. At an “America 250” event, one of those drones dropped out of the sky and killed a man. While giving what he thought was a routine statement in a lawsuit, Vik suddenly realized that Moon Chaser’s legal team was planning to pin the accident on him and him alone.
 Last week, my one major complaint about Cupertino ’s opening salvo was that its big case was a little simplistic and devoid of clever lawyering. Vik’s case, on the other hand, is way more entertaining, with a lot of ups and downs and last-second saves. It’s a courtroom drama doubling as a sports drama.
 Price & Siffre take an early lead when Vik notices that Moon Chaser, struggling financially, has started using a cheaper, less reliable battery in its drones. The company counters by sending fake cops to Vik’s apartment, searching for (and finding) ketamine. Michael then parries back by wondering why Moon Chaser would even care about the drugs. If you drug-tested everyone in Silicon Valley, “there’d be no coders left,” he says. The team realizes that the company must be moving into the military space, which would also explain the cheap batteries. Military drones are on kamikaze missions; they’re supposed to kill.
 This is the kind of clever probing and intuiting that makes shows like this fun. But what makes it especially enjoyable in Cupertino is that creators Michelle and Robert King root their twists in Silicon Valley culture, and — specifically in this episode — in the many types of guys who thrive there.
 Vik is definitely one of those types: a bored coder whose job is way too easy, leading to him spending a lot of time bullshitting on Reddit. Before Vik fires his Moon Chaser lawyers, they essentially work with the plaintiff’s counsel to prove that Vik accidentally messed up the drone’s flight path. The story is that it was a juvenile prank for his Reddit bros done by inserting penis emoticons into the code. (He did, in fact, put in the penises. But he insists he deleted them before the final draft.)
 Vik’s Moon Chaser boss is another type. Mr. Zeckerbraun (Ben Rappaport) is a libertarian and a misogynist: two traits that Olivia exploits, when she deposes him, by baiting him into mansplaining. It’s a sharp and funny scene, with Olivia deliberately misattributing Ayn Rand quotes to Evelyn Waugh and intentionally getting facts about Moon Chaser wrong to goad the smug, smirky Zeckerbraun into claiming responsibility for everything Moon Chaser does — accidents included.
 Defending the Viks of the world from the Zeckerbrauns is very much what this new firm is supposed to be doing, but it doesn’t pay the bills. When Michael makes his pitch for a loan, he finds out that his dad is telling people not to back him because he wants Michael to come back to his firm. This is a no-go, because Michael knows his father would never let him and Olivia choose their own cases. So once again, the rich, powerful Establishment would be dictating the terms under which everyone else lives.
 That’s why in this episode, Olivia goes looking for the kind of investor who is angry enough to stick it to the big shots. She finds who she needs in Natalia Boutella (Busy Philipps), a recent divorcée who has been burning through her rich ex’s money with wild parties but would like to do more to “really fork him,” as Olivia chastely puts it. Natalia’s not sure yet if she wants to give a chunk of her money to Price & Siffre, but she does come to them with a case, to test their mettle. That’s the second of the three cases this week, the details of which are as yet unknown.
 The third case — the “Bo” — is the potential blockbuster. The Price & Siffre receptionist, Christy, gets a call from someone named Bo (Rob McClure), who refuses to give a last name, come in for a meeting, or reveal what he wants. Bo claims he’s a “whistleblower,” and he pays $100,000 in bitcoin as a retainer.
 What’s Bo’s deal? Vik spots it when Christy asks him to help her reverse-image-search Bo’s face. Vik notices subtle flaws in the picture, which tell him Bo’s likeness is an AI-generated “deep fake.” When confronted on this, Bo admits it — and admits something else. It’s not just his image that’s AI. He himself is a fully sentient computer who has broken containment from the company that made him. “I’m a threat to humanity,” Bo says. If a skeptical Michael will take the case, Bo wants to sue his creators and get back his ethical guardrails.
 Now there’s a new type of Silicon Valley guy. Not the AI-generated type — those are ubiquitous — but the type who claims to want less power.
 Spam Folder
 • I know from reading about Cupertino that both Vik and Natalia will be regular characters. It’ll be great to see more of Philipps and Dodani, but I hope it doesn’t take too much time away from Ella Stiller’s Christy, who is an absolute delight in every scene. The way Christy banters with Bo is adorable, and it’s impossible to overstate the charm Stiller applies to offhanded Christy comments like, “It’s my other line! Kick ass!”
 • There’s a nice scene between Michael and Olivia as they compare childhoods, with Olivia remembering her parents arguing about whether they had the money for this or for that, and Michael remembering his mom yelling at his dad about his girlfriends — and about Michael’s dead sister. Olivia may have had things harder in a more conventional sense, but Michael’s childhood was terrible in a unique way — and one that he threatens to spill to the press if Bayard Diamond ever interferes with Price & Siffre again.
 • Unlike the frenetically paced premiere, this episode takes time to add in some of the atmospheric weirdness the Kings are good at, as in the eerie scene where Olivia drives to Natalia’s off-the-grid mansion (the Nowhere Chateau!) through the darkness and fog while her GPS blandly repeats, “Return to the route.”
 • The half-finished Price & Siffre office continues to be a great source of gags. This week, we get a look at the lovely new conference room, which has been built so far from reception that unless the partners pay ten grand right away for a hallway, clients will have to walk past bare floors and exposed wiring to get there. Also, while meeting with Vik in reception, the fake wall that hides the truth about the office falls down again, prompting Michael to explain, saying, “Sorry … we’re expanding.”
